title: Investor Renovation Contractor in Florida | Genstone
metaDescription: Florida investor renovations in Tampa, Orlando, Jacksonville, Miami and more: flips, BRRRR, rentals, 2-4 units, 203(k) and REO, built for wind and flood rules.
intro:
Florida looks like one market from a distance and behaves like five up close. A pier-and-beam bungalow in Jacksonville's Springfield freezes in winter and floods when the St. Johns backs up. A mid-century walk-up in Fort Lauderdale lives under the High-Velocity Hurricane Zone and a cast-iron drain problem. A Cape Coral canal ranch answers to a seawall, a pool cage and a post-Ian flood determination. A Lakeland block house sits on karst. What ties them together is a statewide building code, an insurance system built around four-point and wind mitigation inspections, and a lien law that rewards careful paperwork.

Genstone Construction renovates investment property in Tampa, Orlando, Jacksonville, Miami, St. Petersburg, Fort Lauderdale, Lakeland and Cape Coral for individual investors, lenders, servicers, REITs, funds and Government-Sponsored Enterprises. From our headquarters in Romeoville, Illinois we coordinate vetted, licensed Florida contractors, with a designated field manager on every job. Each project starts with a free Pre-Offer Rehab Review, carries no upfront payment and pays draws only against finished work.

sections.body:
Most of Florida's investable housing was built in three waves, and each wave leaves a predictable repair list.

The land boom of the 1910s and 1920s produced frame bungalows, vernacular cottages and Mediterranean Revival homes in the older cores of Tampa, St. Petersburg, Jacksonville, Orlando, Lakeland and Miami. Many sit on brick piers over crawlspaces. Expect settled foundations, termite damage in sills, knob-and-tube wiring, galvanized supply lines and lead paint.

The postwar decades, roughly the late 1940s through the 1960s, built Florida in concrete block on slabs. Ranches with terrazzo floors, jalousie or awning windows, flat or low-slope roofs in the south and cast-iron drains under the slab fill entire neighborhoods from Fort Lauderdale to Jacksonville's Westside. South Florida added two-story masonry duplexes and walk-up apartment buildings whose exposed concrete now spalls in salt air. Asbestos in floor tile, ceiling texture and mastic is common in this era.

The suburban growth from the 1970s onward added frame-and-block tract homes, polybutylene supply lines in houses from the late 1970s into the mid-1990s and, in some 2006 and 2007 construction, defective imported drywall, concentrated in Southwest Florida. Hurricane Andrew in 1992 split this stock in two: houses built or re-roofed and re-windowed under the post-Andrew codes perform far better in wind than those that were not.

Across all three waves, unpermitted carport enclosures, garage conversions and informal extra units are common, and they affect appraisal, insurance and resale everywhere in the state.

Each Florida region favors different strategies.

In Tampa Bay, flips work best in the bungalow neighborhoods of Seminole Heights, Tampa Heights and St. Petersburg's Kenwood and Old Northeast, where restored character sets the comps. Buy-and-hold investors favor inland block ranches, and since the 2024 storms, the flood map has become the first filter in St. Petersburg and South Tampa.

Central Florida, including Orlando and Lakeland, offers block ranches suited to BRRRR and rentals, historic bungalows around the lakes for flips and owner-occupant 203(k) purchases, and a steady stream of buyers priced out of the coasts. Sinkhole and settlement questions come with the karst geology.

Northeast Florida centers on Jacksonville, where one consolidated city government covers most of Duval County. Springfield and Riverside offer older homes and genuine small multifamily, while Arlington and the Westside supply brick and block rentals.

South Florida, in Miami and Fort Lauderdale, is built around small masonry multifamily and mid-century block homes. Hurricane-code openings, flat roofs, concrete repair and cleanup of unpermitted units drive the budgets, and canal-front lots may be worth more as land than as renovated houses.

Southwest Florida, led by Cape Coral, is a block-home market organized around water access, with seawalls, pool cages, well and septic systems and post-Ian flood rules shaping every scope. Seasonal rentals form a large segment.

REO inventory appears in every region, with flood-damaged homes forming a distinct category along the Gulf Coast since 2022.

Florida runs on a single statewide building code, the Florida Building Code, which local building departments enforce. It is updated on a regular cycle, and it includes specific wind-load requirements for roofs, windows, doors, shutters and screen enclosures. Products in those categories need a Florida product approval, and in Miami-Dade and Broward counties, which form the High-Velocity Hurricane Zone, the requirements are stricter still.

Contractors are licensed through the state's Department of Business and Professional Regulation. General, building, residential, roofing, plumbing and mechanical contractors fall under the Construction Industry Licensing Board, and electrical contractors are licensed separately. Some trades are registered locally. Genstone works only with licensed and insured contractors in each market.

Permits are issued by the city or county where the property sits, and many addresses with a big-city mailing address are actually in an unincorporated county area with its own building department. Locally designated historic districts in several cities add exterior review. In flood zones, building departments compare the cost of the work with the structure's value to decide whether FEMA's substantial improvement rules apply.

Florida's construction lien law adds paperwork that protects owners. Most permitted improvements above a modest value require a recorded Notice of Commencement, and lien waivers from every contractor and supplier keep the title clean. Florida's owner-builder exemption is designed for owners who will occupy the home, so investors renovating for sale or rent generally need licensed contractors. Genstone handles applications, inspections, recording and waivers on every project.

sections.h2: Weather and seasonality in Florida renovation
sections.body:
Florida's weather sets the order of work and, in some markets, the calendar for selling.

The dry season, roughly late fall through spring, is the best time for roofing, exterior painting, concrete repair, seawalls and pool enclosures. It is also when seasonal residents arrive, buyers are most active in the south and southwest and the busiest trades book up. Planning exterior work early in that window matters.

The wet season brings near-daily afternoon thunderstorms, intense lightning, heat and humidity. Roofs are torn off only when they can be dried in the same day, and exterior work shifts to mornings. Any house left closed without air conditioning during these months should be assumed to have mold until proven otherwise.

Hurricane season runs from June through November. A house mid-renovation, with an open roof or missing windows, is vulnerable, so envelope work comes first and materials are secured when storms approach. Recent storms showed that surge can reach far up bays and rivers and that extreme rainfall can flood neighborhoods outside mapped flood zones.

North and Central Florida also see winter freezes. Jacksonville in particular gets hard freezes often enough that exposed plumbing in crawlspaces needs insulation, and vacant houses need heat or winterizing. South Florida never freezes, but salt air and king tides near the coast bring their own maintenance demands.

faqs.q: Which Florida cities does Genstone serve?
faqs.a: We currently coordinate investor renovations in Tampa, Orlando, Jacksonville, Miami, St. Petersburg, Fort Lauderdale, Lakeland and Cape Coral, along with the surrounding communities in each metro. Genstone's headquarters is in Romeoville, Illinois. In Florida we work through a network of vetted, licensed and insured local contractors, with a designated field manager accountable for each project and progress visible without your being on site.

faqs.q: How do Florida insurance inspections affect a renovation?
faqs.a: Heavily. Florida insurers commonly require a four-point inspection covering roof, electrical, plumbing and HVAC on older homes, and they price wind coverage partly on a wind mitigation inspection that looks at roof attachment, roof-to-wall connections and opening protection. A renovation that ignores those reports can leave a house hard to insure, finance or sell. We scope roofs, panels, plumbing and openings with both inspections in mind and document each upgrade.

faqs.q: What is the substantial improvement rule and why does it matter in Florida?
faqs.a: In a FEMA Special Flood Hazard Area, if the cost of repairs or improvements reaches half of the structure's market value, the building must be brought into full compliance with current flood rules, which can mean raising it or rebuilding. After recent hurricanes, Florida building departments have applied this rule to many flood-damaged homes. We check flood zone, any damage determination and structure value before scoping, so the plan is legal.

faqs.q: Do I need to pay anything upfront for a Florida project?
faqs.a: No. Genstone does not take upfront payment. Every project begins with a free Pre-Offer Rehab Review, followed by a detailed scope and estimate with labor, materials and a draw schedule. Construction draws are tied to completed work, and the final payment comes after completion and your approval. Dumpster and debris costs are included in our estimates, and our work carries a one-year workmanship warranty, which excludes tenant damage and normal wear.
